{{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Shrine'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Bitchū Province]].

=== Overview ===
It faces north at the northwest foot of {{ill|Mount Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|qid=Q135646238}} (175 meters above sea level) on the border between {{ill|Bitchū Province|cs|Provincie Biččú|de|Provinz Bitchū|es|Provincia de Bitchū|fa|ولایت بیچو|fi|Bitchūn provinssi|fr|Province de Bitchū|gl|Provincia de Bitchū|id|Provinsi Bitchū|it|Bitchū|ja|備中国|ko|빗추국|lt|Bičiū žemė|nl|Bitchu (provincie)|pt|Província de Bitchū|ru|Биттю (провинция)|simple|Bitchū Province|sk|Biččú|sr|Провинција Бичу|tr|Bitchū (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Біттю|zh|備中國|zh_min_nan|Bittyû-kok|qid=Q1047514}} in the western part of Okayama City. Nakayama in Kibi has been known as {{ill|Sacred mountains|Q1595289|qid=Q1595289}} since ancient times, and Bizen Province Ichinomiya, {{ill|Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|qid=Q500763}}, is enshrined at the northeastern foot of the mountain. Both our company and Kibitsuhiko Shrine enshrine {{ill|Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto|Q65318|qid=Q65318|lt=Okibitsuhiko no Mikoto}}, who is said to have ruled the area, as the main deity, and the clan of life is enshrined here.

Originally, it was the general guardian of {{ill|Kingdom of Kibi|Q1155128|qid=Q1155128}}, but due to the division of Kibikuni into three kingdoms, it became the Ichinomiya of Bichoku, and its branch spirit is the Ichinomiya of Bizen and {{ill|Bingo Province|Q1049113|qid=Q1049113}} (Bizen: Kibitsuhiko Shrine, Bingo: {{ill|Kibitsu Shrine (Bingo)|Q6404042|qid=Q6404042|lt=Kibitsu Shrine}}). For this reason, Kibitsuhiko Shrine in Bizen takes the names of ``Kibisou Chinju'' and ``Sanbi Ichinomiya''. </ref>.The main shrine, which is said to have been built {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Q248381|qid=Q248381}}, is the only {{ill|Kibitsu-zukuri|Q3196321|qid=Q3196321}} (Kibitsu-zukuri) in Japan, and is designated as a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|Q1139795|qid=Q1139795}} along with the worship hall. Additionally, three shrine buildings have been designated as national {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|de|Wichtiges Kulturgut Japans|es|Bien Cultural Importante de Japón|fi|Japanin tärkeä kulttuuriomaisuus|fr|Bien culturel important|id|Properti Kebudayaan Penting (Jepang)|it|Bene culturale importante (Giappone)|ja|重要文化財|ko|일본의 중요문화재|ro|Patrimoniu cultural important al Japoniei|simple|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|th|ทรัพย์สินทางวัฒนธรรมที่สำคัญ (ญี่ปุ่น)|tr|Önemli Kültürel Varlık (Japonya)|uk|Важливі культурні пам'ятки Японії|zh|重要文化財|qid=Q1188622}}. It is also famous for {{ill|narukama shinji|Q11675410|qid=Q11675410}}, which predicts good or bad fortune by the sound of the kettle.<ref name="map" />

It is said that the local politician {{ill|Inukai Tsuyoshi|Q354687|qid=Q354687}} revered Kibitsu Shrine, believing that Inukai Ken-no-Mikoto, the distant ancestor of the Inukai family, was the deity of Okibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto.<ref name="map">{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://okayama-kanko.net/sightseeing/_cms/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/85ba4c00217acc9f333e2c349 6cdce52.pdf|title=Kibiji Tourist Map|publisher=Okayama Tourism and Convention Association|date=|accessdate=2025-01-13|pages=9-10}}</ref>. A bronze statue of Tsuyoshi Inukai was erected on the shore of Kamiike Pond, and the company name of Kibitsu Shrine was also written by Tsuyoshi Inukai.The Spring Festival is held on the second Sunday in May, and the Autumn Festival is held on the second Sunday in October. Among these, the Seventy-Five Zentai Ceremony, in which 75 tables are carried from the Gotoden through the corridor to the main shrine, is one of the three major festivals in Okayama Prefecture. 75 Zentai Shinto ritual|publisher=Okayama Prefecture Tourism Federation|date=|accessdate=2025-11-15|pages=}}</ref>.

"{{ill|Prunus mume|Q157763|qid=Q157763}}", "{{ill|Camellia japonica|Q160121|qid=Q160121}}", "{{ill|Cherry blossom|Q871991|qid=Q871991}}", "{{ill|Paeonia × suffruticosa|Q163018|qid=Q163018|lt=Button}}'', ``{{ill|Rhododendron|Q189393|qid=Q189393}}'', ``{{ill|Rhododendron indicum|Q5366359|qid=Q5366359}}'', ``{{ill|Iris ensata var. ensata|Q21558856|qid=Q21558856}}'', and ``{{ill|Hydrangea macrophylla|Q159219|qid=Q159219}}'', which are also famous flower spots<ref name="map" />. It is also known as a famous spot for {{ill|Autumn leaf color|Q1156320|qid=Q1156320}} in {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|Q43284|qid=Q43284}}.

In ancient times, it was known as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin,'' which consisted of five shrines, the main shrine and four other shrines.

=== History ===

=== Founding ===
[[File:Kibi's Nakayama (from Kibitsu Shrine).JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Enshrined{{ill|Mount Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|qid=Q135646238}}}}{{small|On the far right is the pine trees on the approach. }}]]
According to the shrine's legend, the enshrined deity, Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, lived in a thatched shrine at the foot of {{ill|Mount Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|qid=Q135646238}}, and was buried at the top of the mountain at the age of 281. Regarding the founding of Kibitsu Shrine, there is a theory that it was founded by {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|Q313119|qid=Q313119}} to honor the achievements of Dai Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto, while a shrine legend says that it began when Kayaomi Narumi no Mikoto, the fifth-generation descendant, built a shrine in the thatched shrine and enshrined his life.<ref name="map" />

In the early {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}}, it was donated to {{ill|Ninna-ji|Q1202871|qid=Q1202871}} and became its fief, but during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period}}, control of Ninnaji Temple was threatened due to conflicts<ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the {{ill|Ōnin War|Q385676|qid=Q385676}}, shrine territory was sometimes controlled by the {{ill|Hosokawa clan|Q2736120|qid=Q2736120}}, the protector of Bicchu Province, and the Matsuda clan, a local power.<ref name="Early Modern Period" />At the end of the {{ill|Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}, the power of the {{ill|Mōri clan|Q914637|qid=Q914637}} came to power, and {{ill|Shimizu Muneharu|Q1046032|qid=Q1046032}} and others effectively ruled <ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the unification of the country by {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|af|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ar|تويوتومي هيده-يوشي|arz|تويوتومى هيده يوشى|ast|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|az|Toyotomi Hideyoşi|ban|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|be|Таётомі Хідэёсі|bg|Тойотоми Хидейоши|ca|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|cdo|Hŭng-sìng Séu-gék|ckb|تۆیۆتۆمی ھیدێیۆشی|cs|Hidejoši Tojotomi|de|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|el|Τογιοτόμι Χιντεγιόσι|eo|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|es|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|et|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|eu|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|fa|تویوتومی هیده‌یوشی|fi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|fr|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|gl|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|glk|تویوتومی هیده یوشی|hak|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|he|טויוטומי הידיושי|hr|Tojotomi Hidejoši|hu|Tojotomi Hidejosi|hy|Տոյոտոմի Հիդեյոսի|ia|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|id|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|is|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|it|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|ka|ტოიოტომი ჰიდეიოსი|kk|Тоётоми Хидэёси|ko|도요토미 히데요시|kw|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|la|Taicosama|lt|Tojotomi Hidejoši|lv|Tojotomi Hidejosi|mg|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ml|തൊയൊത്തോമി ഹിദെയോഷി|ms|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|nl|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|no|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|oc|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|pl|Hideyoshi Toyotomi|pt|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ro|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ru|Тоётоми Хидэёси|sc|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|sco|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|simple|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|sk|Hidejoši Tojotomi|sl|Tojotomi Hidejoši|sq|Tojotomi Hidejoshi|sr|Тојотоми Хидејоши|sv|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|tg|Тайетоми Хидзеси|th|โทโยโตมิ ฮิเดโยชิ|tl|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|tr|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|uk|Тойотомі Хідейосі|ur|تویوتومی ہیدیئوشی|vi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|war|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|wuu|丰臣秀吉|zh|丰臣秀吉|zh_classical|豐臣秀吉|zh_min_nan|Toyotomi Hideyosi|zh_yue|豐臣秀吉|zu|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qid=Q187550}}, it became the territory of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hideie Ukita}} and received a donation of shrine territory<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. Furthermore, the ruling relationship with Ninna-ji Temple continued until the early modern period, and it was particularly influenced by rituals.In the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, it first came under the control of the Bicchu magistrate {{ill|Kobori Masatsugu|Q11459515|qid=Q11459515}} as a territory under the direct control of the {{ill|Tokugawa clan|Q1412769|qid=Q1412769}}, and then Miyauchi village, where Kibitsu Shrine is located, became the {{ill|Niwase Domain|Q3034514|qid=Q3034514}} territory.<ref name="Early modern" />. In April of Keicho 6 ({{ill|1601|Q6725|qid=Q6725}}), 160 koku were donated by {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977}}, and after deducting the 60 koku of land removed from the precincts, the total was 100 koku, maintaining the stone height of the Ukita clan era<ref name="Early Modern" />. However, since the {{ill|shuinjō|Q11093673|qid=Q11093673}} was simply written as ``Bicchu Imperial Palace Shinryo,'' there was a dispute between the shrine family and the shrine monks within the shrine over the destination<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. In the 3rd year of Kanbun ({{ill|1663|Q7577|qid=Q7577}}), the ruling of {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|Q1036279|qid=Q1036279}} allowed shrine and family members to manage the main petition, and the red seals from 5th year of Kanbun ({{ill|1665|Q7582|qid=Q7582}}) clearly stated "Kibitsu Daimyo Shrine territory"<ref name="Early modern" />. Even after that, Buddhist facilities such as the {{ill|Three-storied pagoda|Q11357687|qid=Q11357687}} remained in the precincts, and monks continued to read sutras in front of the shrine<ref name="Early Modern Period" />.However, in the 14th year of Kyoho ({{ill|1729|Q6952|qid=Q6952}}), the shrine and family groups requested the temple magistrate to remove the three-storied pagoda, claiming that it was difficult to repair due to age-related deterioration and was dangerous in the event of wind, rain, or earthquakes, and the Buddhist side requested an injunction. The debate between the two leaders went beyond the pros and cons of removing the three-storied pagoda, to whether the shrine should be a syncretistic shrine of Shintoism and Buddhism, or whether the syncretism of Shintoism and Buddhism should be abolished as the only Shinto shrine.<ref name="Early Modern Period" /> The temple magistrate was the only one who did not directly judge whether it was Shinto or not, but it approved the removal of the three-storied pagoda, denied that the temple had anything to do with the shrine, and determined that the temple had no qualifications to sue. Buddhist buildings such as the three-storied pagoda have disappeared from maps of the precincts from the Kyoho period onward, and it is believed that the separation of Shinto and Buddhism was completed during this period.

=== Precincts ===

=== Main shrine and worship hall ===
[[File:Kibitsu Jinja -01.jpg|thumb|400px|right|{{center|Main shrine and worship hall (national treasure)}}]]The existing main shrine and worship hall were built in the first year of {{ill|Meitoku|Q1145032|qid=Q1145032}} of the {{ill|Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845}} ({{ill|1390|Q6375|qid=Q6375}}) under the orders of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōgon|Q555465|qid=Q555465}}.{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Muromachi Shogunate}}The third shogun Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381}} started construction and moved to {{ill|Ōei|Q1193078|qid=Q1193078}} in 1425.<ref>[http://www.kibitujinja.com/about/honden.html Shrine official website], [http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=4 "Okayama's Cultural Properties"] (Okayama Prefecture website), [https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/195650 Cultural Heritage Online] etc. indicate that the main shrine was built in 1425 ({{ill|1425|Q6283|qid=Q6283}}). ``Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia Japan's National Treasures'' No. 29 (Asahi Shimbun, 1997) states that the main shrine was completed in the 12th year of Oei ({{ill|1405|Q6124|qid=Q6124}}), and that the temporary roof was replaced with cypress bark in the 32nd year of Oei, and the shrine was officially transferred to the shrine. </ref>. A gabled and flat worship hall is connected to the front of the main hall, which is built with a gabled gable structure. Hiyoku Irimoya-zukuri is a roof style in which two {{ill|East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Q855025|qid=Q855025}} roofs are arranged one behind the other, and is also called ``Kibitsu-zukuri.''The size of the main shrine is comparable to the main shrine of {{ill|Izumo-taisha|Q696362|qid=Q696362}} and {{ill|Yasaka Shrine|Q692714|qid=Q692714}}, and the influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen everywhere. It is one step higher than the ground, and is built on a stucco-coated earthen platform (Kamebukuro), with a floor plan of 5 ken in the front, 7 ken in the back, and 8 ken in beam space, and the roof is {{ill|cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477}}. Inside, there is a closed inner hall in the center and an inner hall in front of it, surrounded by a lower middle hall, and in front of the middle hall is an even lower vermillion platform (Akenodan), which is surrounded by an even lower outer hall. In this way, it has a unique structure in which the floor height gradually increases from the outside to the inside. The upper half of the wall is surrounded by renji windows, which are rare for shrines. It is said to be the only example of {{ill|Daibutsuyō|Q3012037|qid=Q3012037}} (daibutsuyo) applied to the main hall of a shrine, such as the shape of the inset wood, the bowl, and the rainbow beam.

The worship hall was built at the same time as the main shrine, with three girders (side lines) and one beam (front) with gables; the front is gabled and the back is connected to the main shrine. There are mokoshi floors on the front and sides. The roof is made of cypress bark like the main hall, but the lower floor is made of tile. These main shrines and worship halls are designated as {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|Q1139795|qid=Q1139795}}. - 283</ref><ref name="Main shrine and worship hall"/>.

=== Other shrine buildings ===
* Okamaden
*: {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}}11 ({{ill|1606|Q6747|qid=Q6747}}) Rebuilt by miner Chitane Yasuhara. Single-story, flat-sided roof with real tiles. It is a rectangular shape extending north and south, with a cauldron placed in the north two spaces. A special ritual called "{{ill|narukama shinji|Q11675410|qid=Q11675410}}" is held every day except Friday. <ref name="Okamaden"/> has been designated as a national important cultural property.
* Corridor
*: It is said to have been built during {{ill|Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}, between {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}} ({{ill|1573|Q6678|qid=Q6678}} - {{ill|1591|Q6766|qid=Q6766}}). Total length 398 meters. <ref name="Corridor"/> has been designated as a cultural property by Okayama Prefecture.
* Kitazuishinmon
*: Rebuilt in 11 ({{ill|1542|Q6520|qid=Q6520}}) during the Muromachi period. Single-layer gabled cypress bark roof. It was built on the approach from the front of the shrine. <ref name="Kitazuishinmon"/> has been designated as a national important cultural property.
* Minamizuishinmon*: Reconstruction in {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period}}, {{ill|Enbun|Q1145071|qid=Q1145071}}2 ({{ill|1357|Q6135|qid=Q6135}}). The oldest Kibitsu Shrine. Single-layer gable roof with tile roof. It was built in the middle of the corridor to Hongu Shrine. <ref name="Minamizuishinmon"/> is designated as a national important cultural property.

=== Setsusha ===
[[File:Hongu Shrine (Kibitsu Shrine precinct shrine).JPG|right|thumb|200px|{{center|Hongu Shrine}}]]
It is said that in ancient times there were five shrine buildings and 72 subsidiary shrines. The five shrine buildings (Main Shrine, Hongu Shrine, Shingu Shrine, Naiku Shrine, and Iwayama Shrine) are collectively referred to as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin''. </ref>. {{ill|2025|Q49616|qid=Q49616}} ({{ill|Reiwa era|Q62609017|qid=Q62609017}}7) Currently, Shingu Shrine and Naiku Shrine are enshrined in Hongu Shrine.
* Hongu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: {{ill|Emperor Kōrei|Q313041|qid=Q313041}} (7th generation. Father of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto).
** Shingu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kibi Takehiko no Mikoto (son of Wakahiko Kenkibitsu Hiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was enshrined in Higashiyama in the south until the end of the Meiji period.
** Naiku Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Hyakuta Yumiya Hime no Mikoto (wife of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was originally enshrined on the mountain in the southern part of {{ill|Mount Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|qid=Q135646238}}.
* Sanshagu - A collective term for the following three companies.
** Kasuga Shrine
** Daijingu Shrine
** Hachiman Shrine
* Iwayama Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kenhikkatabetsu no Mikoto (landlord deity of Kibi Province).
* Taki Matsuri Shrine
* Ebisusha
*Soreisha Shrine
* Ichidosha
* Uga Shrine - Enshrined on the island of Kamiike.

Total length 377.3 cm, blade length 226.7 cm, warp 5 cm, weight 13 kg. Hog-zukuri, round building. The largest Japanese sword in Japan during the Koto period. Although there is no evidence that it was used as a votive sword, the entire blade is hardened, the {{ill|nakago|Q1963918|qid=Q1963918|lt=stem}} is long, and the three mekugi holes are evenly spaced, indicating that it was made with actual combat in mind.

يىلى|uk|2021|ur|2021ء|uz|2021|vec|2021|vi|2021|vls|2021|vo|2021|wa|2021|war|2021|wuu|2021年|xmf|2021|yi|2021|yo|2021|za|2021 nienz|zea|2021|zgh|2021|zh|2021年|zh_classical|二〇二一年|zh_min_nan|2021 nî|zh_yue|2021年|zu|2021|qid=Q49628}} ({{ill|Reiwa era|Q62609017|qid=Q62609017}}3) From January 15th to 22nd, it was discovered that someone had made linear scratches on the pillars of the shrine's worship hall and corridor. In February of the same year, a suspect who had damaged {{ill|Matsuyama Castle (Iyo)|Q981357|qid=Q981357}} and {{ill|Kōchi Castle|Q1012815|qid=Q1012815}} was arrested for violating {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|Q1188502|qid=Q1188502}}, and was arrested again for committing similar crimes at Kibitsu Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|date=2021-02-13 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210213122041/https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2021021300375&g=soc |title=Rearrest of 47-year-old man suspected of damaging Kibitsu Shrine - Okayama Prefectural Police |website=Jiji Press|publisher=Jiji Press|accessdate=2021-02-13}} {{ja icon}}</ref>.

'''Access'''
* Railway
** {{ill|West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|qid=Q502125}} (JR West) {{ill|Kibi Line|Q844682|qid=Q844682}} {{ill|Kibitsu Station|ja|吉備津駅|jv|Setatsiyun Kibitsu|ko|기비쓰역|my|ခိဘိဆွတ်ဘူတာ|zh|吉備津站|qid=Q6404041}} (10 minutes walk)
* bus
**Take the {{ill|Bihoku Bus|Q11387355|qid=Q11387355}} (bound for "Jito" via {{ill|Higashi-Sōja Station|Q3661745|qid=Q3661745|lt=Higashisoja}}) and get off at the "Kibitsu Shrine Sandoguchi" bus stop (2 minutes walk after getting off)
**<s>Take the {{ill|Chutetsu Bus|Q11367772|qid=Q11367772}} (bound for {{ill|Japan National Route 180|Q6156873|qid=Q6156873}} towards "Kibitsu Shrine") and get off at the last stop of "Kibitsu Shrine" (short walk after getting off)</s> (Currently suspended)
**<s>Take the Chutetsu bus (bound for National Route 180 towards "Inariyama" or "Oi") and get off at the "Kibitsu Shrine Sandoguchi" bus stop (2 minutes walk after getting off)</s> (currently suspended)

'''Surroundings'''
[[File:Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun, haisho.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun|Q11364273|qid=Q11364273}}}}{{small|The Imperial Household Agency-regulated tomb of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto. }}]]* {{ill|Mount Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|qid=Q135646238}}
*: Many ancient tombs and ancient ritual sites remain in Nakayama, Kibi, at the rear of the temple grounds, and it is believed that it was worshiped as {{ill|Sacred mountains|Q1595289|qid=Q1595289}} since ancient times. At the summit of Mt. Chausu (160 meters) in the center, there is an ancient tomb believed to be the grave of Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, and at the summit of the highest peak, Mt. Ryuo (northern peak, 175 meters above sea level), there is {{ill|Iwakura rock|Q11587880|qid=Q11587880}}, where Kibitsuhiko Shrine is enshrined.
** {{ill|Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun|Q11364273|qid=Q11364273}} ​​- {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|Q11268718|qid=Q11268718}} with a length of 120 meters. It has been designated by the Imperial Household Agency as the ``Grave of Great Kibitsuhiko.''
** Kibi Archaeological Museum
* {{ill|Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|qid=Q500763}} - Bizen Province Ichinomiya.
* Remains of the residence of the Kayo clan - Believed to be the site of the residence of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kayō clan}} who served as a priest at Kibitsu Shrine. Okayama Prefecture's designated historic site <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=325 Dengayoujikan Ruins] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
* {{ill|Eisai|Q366128|qid=Q366128|lt=Eishi}}Monument of the birthplace of the monk
* {{ill|Tsukuriyama Kofun (Okayama)|Q11639745|qid=Q11639745}} - The 4th largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in Japan.
